title: Environments, Configuration & Rollback
objectives: Define environment promotion and what may differ between environments
Inject configuration and secrets at deploy time rather than baking them in
Gate deploys on health checks before declaring success
Contrast container rollback with desktop (Tauri) release and update flow
body:
The deploy finished. Is the software working? A pipeline that stops at 'image pushed, container started' has shipped nothing — it has shipped a hope. Production maturity is measured between 'deployed' and 'verified, with a rollback path you have actually rehearsed'.

## The problem

The same artifact must behave correctly in three places with three data sets, three secret sets and three risk tolerances. Constraints: no rebuilds per environment, no secrets in artifacts, no deploy declared done before evidence, and a way back that is faster than the way forward.

## Environment promotion

Commits flow dev → staging → production, and the artifact moves forward unchanged — only configuration differs. What legitimately differs: database endpoints and credentials, replica counts, resource limits, TLS termination, log levels. What must never differ: the image, the schema-migration discipline, the config mechanism. If you cannot say what differs between staging and prod, you cannot reason about what a staging green light means.

## Configuration injection

Config enters at runtime:

```yaml
# deploy snippet — configuration and secrets are runtime input
environment:
  DATABASE_URL: $DATABASE_URL       # secret manager -> env
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: "true"
image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:9f2c...   # pinned digest, not :latest
```

The digest pin matters for rollback: tags are mutable pointers (someone can re-push :v1.4.2), digests are immutable. Rolling 'back' to a moved tag can deploy the wrong bytes.

## Health-gated deploys

Deploy is not done when the container starts; it is done when evidence says so:

1. New instances come up beside old ones.
2. Readiness probes pass (dependency reachable, migrations applied) before traffic shifts.
3. Canary or percentage rollout; watch error rate and latency against the old version.
4. All-traffic cutover; old instances drain and terminate.
5. If gates fail at any point: automatic rollback to the previous image.

Liveness ('is it wedged? restart it') must stay a different, cheaper check than readiness ('can it serve?'). Mixing them creates restart storms during dependency outages.

## Rollback strategy

A rollback you have never rehearsed is a rumor. The requirements: the previous artifact still exists (registry retention, app-store version history), migrations are expand/contract so the old code can run against the new schema, and the switch itself is one action (repoint a load balancer, restart at previous digest, re-publish previous app version). Define rollback time — how long until you are back to good — per service, and test it quarterly.

## What 'deploy' means: containers vs desktop

The word hides two different release models:

- **Server/container** — you control the fleet: push a digest, shift traffic, roll back in minutes; users never act.
- **Desktop (e.g. Tauri)** — the 'server' is the users' machines: you ship installers (msi, dmg, AppImage) and updates via a signed update feed; users (or their auto-updater) adopt at their own pace; rollback means publishing a corrected version and waiting for propagation. There is no traffic shifting — version skew across the fleet is permanent, so the API and file formats need backward compatibility the server side can sometimes dodge.

Same pipeline anatomy — build, test, package, release — but the deploy and rollback mechanics differ completely, and desktop demands signing keys and update-feed infrastructure that servers never need.

## Best practices

- Deploy by digest; treat tags as human labels only.
- Readiness gates traffic; liveness guards wedges. Never merge them.
- Keep expand/contract migrations so the previous release can run on the current schema.
- Rehearse rollback quarterly with a game day; measure time-to-restore.
- Canary with automatic analysis (error rate, latency) rather than hope-based full rollout.
- For desktop, sign releases and version the update feed from day one.

## Common mistakes

- Declaring success on 'container running' with zero health verification.
- Rolling back code without checking schema compatibility — instant second outage.
- Config drift: staging tweaked by hand until it proves nothing about prod.
- Shipping secrets baked into artifacts because injection felt like work.
- Treating desktop releases like server deploys and having no update-feed rollback path.

examples.name: deploy-and-update.yaml
examples.code:
# --- container deploy: health-gated, digest-pinned, reversible ---
release:
  image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:9f2c7e...   # immutable
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10                      # 10% of traffic
        - pause: { duration: 2m }            # watch error rate & p95
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
  readinessProbe:
    httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3000 }    # gates traffic
  livenessProbe:
    httpGet: { path: /live, port: 3000 }     # restarts wedged pods
  rollback:
    trigger: analysisFailed                  # automatic
    previousImage: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:41ab9d...

# --- desktop release (Tauri-style): ship + signed update feed ---
# pipeline tail:
#   build: npm run tauri build   -> .msi, .dmg, .AppImage
#   sign: release artifacts + update manifest (minisign / code signing)
#   publish: upload installers; publish latest.json to the update feed
# rollout: auto-updaters pull latest.json on launch; users adopt
#          gradually -> version skew is the steady state
# rollback: publish a corrected version to the feed (can't un-ring
#           installed copies; server API must stay backward compatible)

exercise.prompt: Plan a release across two artifact worlds. Write planRelease(release) in JavaScript: given a target (desktop or container) and steps with a type (build/test/package/publish/deploy), mark each step SHIP or SKIP for that target — containers deploy from a registry, desktop apps publish to an update feed — and add a rollbackStrategy line per world. Render the plan.
hints: Desktop world: the artifact ships through a signed update feed, not a registry deploy.
Container world: the digest is deployed to the fleet; there is no update feed.
The rollback line differs: repoint to previous digest vs publish a corrected version.

questions.prompt: What is the key operational difference between deploying a container and releasing a desktop app update?
options: Containers shift traffic and roll back in minutes on infrastructure you control; desktop updates propagate via a feed at users' pace, with permanent version skew
Desktop apps cannot be rolled back at all
Containers require code signing, desktop apps do not
questions.explanation: You control the fleet: digest pinning plus traffic shifting gives fast, reversible deploys. On desktop, adoption is user-paced and rolled-forward — so backward compatibility of the API is mandatory.

questions.prompt: Why deploy by image digest (sha256:...) instead of a tag like :v1.4.2?
options: Tags are mutable pointers that can be re-pushed; digests are immutable, so rollback means the exact previous bytes
questions.explanation: A tag can be silently re-pushed, so 'rolling back to the tag' can deploy the wrong bits. A digest pins the artifact content itself.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of probes is correct for a health-gated deploy?
options: Use one endpoint for both liveness and readiness
Readiness gates traffic ('can it serve?'); liveness restarts wedged processes ('is it stuck?')
Liveness gates traffic; readiness restarts the pod
Neither is needed if the container started
questions.explanation: Merging them causes restart storms during dependency outages. Readiness asks whether to send traffic; liveness asks whether the process is wedged and needs a restart.
